summary: Explains why the Connection-less Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CLDAP) specification, RFC 1798, was never advanced beyond Proposed Standard, and recommends that it be moved to Historic status.

eli5.summary: A little-used way to ask a directory questions never grew popular. This document says it should be officially retired and moved to the history shelf.

questions: why was connectionless ldap made historic
subtitle: Why the connection-less flavour of LDAP never caught on, and why RFC 1798 was retired to Historic.

tldr.problem: CLDAP, specified in RFC 1798 in 1995, was meant for quick directory lookups without a connection, but it stalled and could not stay on the standards track.
tldr.mechanism: This memo lists the likely reasons for its lack of deployment and recommends that RFC 1798 be moved to Historic status.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1798 is retired. People interested in connection-less directory access are pointed to experiment with other approaches.

today: RFC 3352 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1798 by recommending that CLDAP be moved to Historic status. It has not been obsoleted itself.

sections.title: What CLDAP Was
sections.content:
Connection-less LDAP (CLDAP, RFC 1798) was published in 1995 as a Proposed Standard. It targeted applications that look up small amounts of information held in a directory. It skipped the cost of opening and closing a connection, and the bind and unbind operations that connection-oriented directory protocols need.

It was designed to complement version 2 of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAPv2, RFC 1777), which is itself now Historic.
sections.eli5: CLDAP was a way to ask a quick question without first knocking, saying hello and signing in. Like shouting a question across the street instead of making a phone call.

sections.title: Why It Did Not Take Off
sections.content:
Seven years after publication, the memo says CLDAP had not become widely deployed on the Internet. It lists probable reasons:

  • Limited functionality: anonymous only, read only, and small result sizes only.
  • Insufficient security: no integrity protection and no confidentiality protection.
  • Inadequate internationalization support and insufficient extensibility.
  • A lack of multiple independently developed implementations.

There was also a standards-process problem. The specification has normative references to several obsolete specifications, including RFC 1487, the predecessor of RFC 1777. Without an update, it could not remain on the standards track because of the normative reference to a Historic RFC.
sections.eli5: It could only ask, never change anything, and anyone could listen in. Few people built it, and its old rule book pointed at other rule books that had been thrown out.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
The IETF chartered the LDAP Extensions Working Group in 1997 to update CLDAP. That group was concluding without producing an update, and no standardization effort remained. The community still wanted a connection-less directory protocol, but considered further experimentation necessary, in particular on the security issues of connection-less services.

The memo therefore says RFC 1798 must be moved to Historic status. It suggests that people interested in connection-less access to X.500-based directory services experiment with LDAP over UDP and other alternatives.
sections.eli5: Nobody was going to fix it, so it goes on the history shelf. People who still like the idea are told to try new versions instead.
